---
title: Reading back and discovery
---

## Reads need one Sign

Every Sign that matches a Packet's Sign Type and Sign Address acts on it. For a
write that is harmless; for a read, every matching Sign answers at once and the
answers collide. So a read to Sign Address 0 (the default) or to a `?` pattern
raises `ValueError`, and nothing is sent.

Give the `Sign` the Sign's own address:

```python
sign = Sign.serial("/dev/ttyUSB0", model=models.ALPHA_4120C, address=1)
```

If only one Sign is on the line, you can keep address 0 and allow reads anyway:

```python
sign = Sign.serial("/dev/ttyUSB0", broadcast_reads=True)
```

## What you can read

```python
sign.read_text("A")             # Message
sign.read_string("T")           # tuple of Segments
sign.read_dots_picture("P")     # DotsPicture
sign.info()                     # GeneralInformation
sign.serial_errors()            # SerialErrorStatus
```

The display pauses while the Sign answers a read.

`info()` reports the firmware part number, revision, and date, the Sign's clock and
time format, whether the speaker is on, and the total and free memory:

```python
info = sign.info()
print(info.firmware, info.revision, info.memory_free, "of", info.memory_total)
```

On a 4120C the free figure is the room left in the first TEXT File, less 5 bytes,
so it does not always match what the Memory Configuration leaves free.

## Did the data arrive?

The Sign records serial errors: a bad Checksum, a buffer overflow, a framing error
(usually a baud rate mismatch), and an illegal Command or File Label.
`serial_errors()` reads the record and resets it, so each read covers what was sent
since the one before:

```python
sign.write_string("T", "72F")
status = sign.serial_errors()
if not status.ok:
    print(status)
```

A 4120C sets the overflow bit when a TEXT File write is longer than the File, and
the illegal command bit when a STRING File write is longer than the File.

## Timeouts and late answers

A read waits `read_timeout` seconds (2 by default) for each part of the answer, and
raises `SignTimeoutError` if nothing comes. The usual causes are a wrong Sign
Address or Sign Type, the wrong line settings, or a cable that carries data only
toward the Sign.

If an answer arrives after its read timed out, the next read skips it. A late
answer to the same kind of read can't be told apart from the real one, which is
one more reason to give each Sign its own address.

A damaged answer raises `ResponseError`, a `ValueError`.

## Find the Signs on a line

`discover` asks every Sign on the line for its Sign Type and Sign Address. It takes
a Transport rather than a `Sign`, because it reaches every Sign Type:

```python
from alpha_led_sign import SerialTransport, discover

with SerialTransport("/dev/ttyUSB0") as line:
    for found in discover(line, max_address=15):
        print(found.address, found.sign_type, found.model)
```

`found.model` is the Sign Model with that Sign Type, when exactly one has it.

Each Sign answers in turn, 1 s + 0.5 s × its address after the query, so discovery
waits for the highest address you ask about, plus 1 s. All 255 addresses
take over two minutes; `max_address=15` takes about 9.5 s. A Sign ignores other
Commands until it has answered.

Two Signs that share an address garble each other's answers. Discovery skips a
garbled answer with a warning.

## Give a Sign its own address

```python
sign = Sign.serial("/dev/ttyUSB0", model=models.ALPHA_4120C)   # address 0
sign.set_sign_address(1, broadcast=True)
```

Sent to address 0, this reaches every matching Sign on the line and gives them all
the same address, so the library refuses unless you pass `broadcast=True`. Do it
with one Sign connected. Afterwards the `Sign` object sends to the new address.

A Sign Address set with DIP switches takes over again after a power cycle.
